name: SAM (Security Account Manager) Hive
os_min: Windows 2000 (present in all NT-based Windows versions)
purpose: Stores local user account definitions for the machine — RIDs, group memberships, and encrypted password hashes — plus per-account login metadata. It is unreadable in place even by local Administrator while Windows is running; access requires SYSTEM privileges or an offline copy.
key_fields: SAM\Domains\Account\Users\<RID in 8-digit hex> — one subkey per local account (e.g. 000001F4 = RID 500)
V value — username, full name, comment, and the encrypted LM/NT hash blob
F value — account flags and timestamps: last logon, password last set, account expires, failed-logon count
SAM\Domains\Account\Users\Names — maps account name to RID
SAM\Domains\Builtin\Aliases — builtin group (e.g. Administrators, RID 544) membership
normal_baseline: RID 500 is the built-in Administrator (often renamed and/or disabled per hardening baselines); RID 501 is the built-in Guest (disabled by default); real user accounts start at RID 1000 and increment sequentially as created. F-value timestamps track plausibly with the account's known usage and the org's password-rotation policy.
anomalies: RID hijacking: the F value of a low-privilege or disabled account (commonly Guest, RID 501) is patched so the account authenticates with the Administrator's RID (500) SID, granting admin rights while `net user`/account-listing tools still show it as Guest.
The built-in Administrator account (RID 500) is enabled when the environment's baseline/GPO expects it disabled.
A new local account's RID or last-write time doesn't fit the expected sequential/temporal pattern for how accounts are normally provisioned on that host.
An account newly added to a privileged builtin alias (e.g. Administrators) shortly before or during suspicious activity.
F-value 'last logon' or 'password last set' timestamps inconsistent with the account's known usage window.
anti_forensic_notes: Password hashes in the SAM are encrypted with a boot key derived from the paired SYSTEM hive; a SAM hive collected without its matching SYSTEM hive cannot be decrypted. Attackers with SYSTEM-level access can dump SAM via `reg save`, Volume Shadow Copies (bypassing the live file lock), or in-memory extraction (e.g. Mimikatz lsadump::sam), leaving little or no on-disk trace beyond the access itself. RID hijacking abuses the F-value structure directly, so it will not show up in standard account-enumeration output and requires binary inspection of the F value to detect.
